```{python}
import polars as pl 
import numpy as np
from lets_plot import *
import polars.selectors as cs

LetsPlot.setup_html(isolated_frame=True)

data_url = "https://byuidatascience.github.io/DS250-Course-Polars/Data/StarWars_with_emails.csv"
```

<!-- The first 10 rows are not part of the datset we need.

The columns headers are split across two rows. We need to clean and simplify the column headers-->

```{python}
# Read in and tidy up the first row
a = pl.Series(pl.read_csv(data_url, skip_rows = 10, n_rows=1, has_header=False, encoding = 'utf8-lossy').row(0))
# Note the non-aschii character in the column "Do you consider yourself to be a fan of the Expanded Universe". (column AF if you open it in Excel). 

# BTW: Detecting what it is and where can be difficult

# Lossy means that invalid utf8 values are replaced with � characters. When using other encodings than utf8 or utf8-lossy, the input is first decoded in memory with python. Defaults to utf8...ignore_errors = True does not replace the non-utf8 character with a blank space like you would hope

a[2] = "seen_any" #simply overwrite the value at index 2

# Rather than changing each column header manually,
# here we use regex to apply changes more efficiently
a = (
  a.str.replace(r".+seen.+", "seen_")
   .str.replace(r".+rank.+", "rank_")
   .str.replace(r"(.+favorably.+)", "fav_")
   .fill_null(strategy = "forward")

   .str.replace("\uFFFD+", "") #this gets rid of the question marks in a diamond characters 
   .str.strip_chars()
   .str.to_lowercase()
   .str.replace_all(" ", "_")
   .str.replace(r"location(.+)", "location")

)
a[3] = "star_wars_fan"
a[30] = "who_shot_first"
a[31] = "know_expanded_universe"
a[32] = "expanded_universe_fan"
a[33] = "star_trek_fan"
```

<!-- Combine series q and a into one series to be used as column names-->

```{python}
b = pl.Series(pl.read_csv(data_url, skip_rows = 11, n_rows=1, has_header=False, encoding = 'utf8-lossy').row(0))

b = (
  b.str.replace(r"Star Wars: (Episode \w+) .+", "${1}")
   .str.replace("Response", "")
   .str.replace_all(" ", "_")
   .fill_null("")
   .str.strip_chars()
)

```

```{python}
#Now combine the two series, each of which contains part of the desired column header
new_names = (a + b).to_list()

# Read in the data, skipping over the column header rows
# and use 'new_names' as the column headers
df = pl.read_csv(data_url, skip_rows=12, has_header=False, new_columns = new_names )
```




# Task 1 (regex)

```{python}
# display(df.schema)
```

```{python}
# here I created first and last name as well as the email domain
df_new = df.with_columns(
  pl.col("email").str.extract(r"^([a-zA-Z]+)", 1).str.strip_chars().alias("first_name"),
  pl.col("email").str.extract(r"[._\d]([a-zA-Z]+)@", 1).str.strip_chars().alias("last_name"),
  pl.col("email").str.extract(r"@(.+)$", 1).str.to_lowercase().str.strip_chars().alias("email_domain")
)

# df_new 
```


```{python}
df_new.group_by("email_domain").len().sort("len", descending=True)

# 707 gmail
# 286 myorg
# 193 yahoo

df = df_new
df_nonML = df
```

# Task 2 (Data cleaning & prep for ML)

```{python}
# age to int
df_ml = df_new.filter(pl.any_horizontal(pl.col(r"^seen_Episode.*$").is_not_null()))


# print(df_ml.shape)

df_ml1 = df_ml.with_columns(
  pl.col('age').str.extract(r"(\d+)", 1).cast(pl.Int32).alias("age_int")
).drop('age')

```

```{python}
# education to int
df_ml2 = df_ml1.with_columns(
    pl.col("education").replace_strict({
        "Less than high school degree": 1,
        "High school degree": 2,
        "Some college or Associate degree": 3,
        "Bachelor degree": 4,
        "Graduate degree": 5
    }).alias("education_int")
)

# table to show the education -> education_int mapping actually applied
display(df_ml2.select("education", "education_int").unique().sort("education_int"))

df_ml2 = df_ml2.drop("education")
```

```{python}
df_ml3 = df_ml2.with_columns(
    pl.col("household_income").str.replace_all(r",", "").str.extract(r"^\$([\d]+)", 1).cast(pl.Int32).alias("income_int")
).drop("household_income")

# df_ml3['income_int']
```

```{python}
# df_ml3.group_by("fav_Han_Solo").agg(pl.len())

df = df_ml3.with_columns(
    cs.starts_with("fav_").replace_strict({
        "Very unfavorably": 1,
        "Somewhat unfavorably": 2,
        "Neither favorably nor unfavorably (neutral)": 3,
        "Somewhat favorably": 4,
        "Very favorably": 5,
        "Unfamiliar (N/A)": 0
    })
)

```


# Task 3 (ML)

```{python}
# Include and execute your code here
df = df.filter(pl.any_horizontal(pl.col(r"^seen_Episode.*$").is_not_null()))
```

```{python}
df = df.with_columns(
    (pl.col("income_int") >= 50000).cast(pl.Int8).alias("high_income")
).drop_nulls("high_income")
```

```{python}
# drop columns that we arent training on
#df.drop(['respondentid', 'email', 'first_name', 'last_name'])# .to_dummies('domain').head(5)
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# drop strings and target column
x = df.select(cs.numeric()).drop(["respondentid", "income_int", "high_income"]).to_numpy()


y = df.select("high_income").to_numpy().ravel()

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(x, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=42) 

clf = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42, max_depth=5, min_samples_leaf=20)
clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
pred = clf.predict(X_test)

```

```{python}
# feature importance table + chart
feature_names = df.select(cs.numeric()).drop(["respondentid", "income_int", "high_income"]).columns

importance_df = pl.DataFrame({
    "feature": feature_names,
    "importance": clf.feature_importances_
}).sort("importance", descending=True).head(10)

display(importance_df)

display(
  ggplot(importance_df, aes(x="feature", y="importance"))
  + geom_bar(stat="identity")
  + labs(title="Top 10 Feature Importances", x="Feature", y="Importance")
  + theme_classic()
  + theme(axis_text_x=element_text(angle=45, hjust=1))
)
```

```{python}
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report
print(classification_report(y_test, pred))
```

## Executive Summary

I went through the provided Star Wars survey data and created a cleaned dataframe that I used to build a classification model to predict if any given person in the data made more then $50K a year. 

I have not yet done the stretch task.

## Methods

I used regular expressions to create a first, last names column and also to extract the email domain from the email column. After regex I filtered the data to those who had seen at least 1 of the Star Wars movies. After that I preped the data for ML by converting what string I should to numeric values. After that I dropped rows with nulls and columns with strings. Then I trained a decision tree classifier and printed out its report.


## Results

The ML model got 66% accuracy on the test set.

```{python}
print(classification_report(y_test, pred))
```

## Conclusion 

With the given data I was able to create a model that could predict if someone makes more then $50K a year with 66% accuracy. Thats only 16% accuracy over guessing, so I learned that predicting income based on if someone likes Star Wars isnt a great way to do it.

The top 5 best features for predicting income are:
- age_int
- education_int
- fav_Anakin_Skywalker
- fav_Jar_Jar_Binks
- rank_Episode_V

The feature importance chart confirms this: age_int and education_int are by far the two most important features. (Both of which dont even have to do with Star Wars)

As for the content itself, we can learn that the category of people who watch Star Wars movies most is 45-60 year olds. Males are slightly more likely to have seen the films than females.
